title: You Hit the Bull's Eye, but Was It the Right Bull? (Start With Why)
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain's argument is that hitting a target proves nothing if the target was wrong, and that most people and most organisations get lost in the How and the What without ever settling the Why. He reports asking the question of job candidates, new hires and conference audiences and getting a blank stare or a half-hearted ramble in return, which he treats as evidence of how rarely the question is worked through. The piece then runs three parallel analogies - captain of a transatlantic cruise ship, leader of a business unit, and an individual with personal ambitions - through each layer in turn. The Why is defined as vision: a manifestation of core ideals and the reason you get up in the morning, and the thing that keeps both crew and customers committed. The What is the goal aligned to that vision, with measures attached, whether that is OKRs for a quarter or a personal target for the year. The How is the roadmap, and Jain adds the leadership-specific instruction that the leader should largely stay out of it and give teams autonomy over execution. His closing move is that the Why is not a one-time artefact but something a leader must keep restating so the organisation stays pointed in the right direction.
points: The governing claim is sequencing: vision must be crafted and articulated before priorities, goals or roadmaps are touched, because the alternative is executing efficiently toward the wrong target.
Jain uses the blank stares he gets when asking candidates and new hires about their Why as evidence that the question is almost never worked through in advance.
The three-analogy structure - ship captain, business leader, individual - is the piece's usable device, letting the same why/what/how test be run on an organisation and on a personal life.
He insists on measures attached to the What, whether key results in an OKR model or a dated personal target, so that alignment to the vision is checkable rather than asserted.

The leadership instruction buried in the How section is delegation: the leader typically should not be in the execution plan at all, but should give teams autonomy to carve out the processes that reach the goal.
quotes: I love to ask this question to candidates at job interviews, to all new members joining my organization, and also people I meet at seminars and conferences. And in a majority of cases what I get in return is a blank stare, or at most a half-hearted ramble.

In today’s fast-paced, highly competitive environment it is easy to get sucked into execution, and lose sight of the bigger picture. When starting a company, managing a group, or working toward personal objectives, we tend to prioritize the nuts-and-bolts before we know which direction we’re heading.
Your “why” is the reason you get up in the morning. It is a manifestation of your core ideals, priorities, and interests. It is your vision.

As a leader in an organization, your first task should be to craft and articulate your organization’s vision, or to reiterate it if it’s already defined. You need to make sure your entire organization understands the vision, and are inspired by it.
Your “How” is the roadmap, the blueprint that charts your path to the objective. The roadmap is only possible to build if you are clear of the outcomes, the objectives, the goals.

Starting with Why ensures you choose the right direction and the goals that make most sense for your situation. But the Why shouldn’t be forgotten once it is defined, and instead should be revisited to make sure you are always headed in the right direction.
